questions.question: A student council survey asks: 'Do you agree that our tired old playground should be replaced?' Thirty students answered it. What is the main problem with this survey?
options: The words 'tired old' push students toward answering yes
Nothing is wrong; 30 answers is enough to balance out any bias
Nothing is wrong; students could still answer no if they wanted
The survey should have asked about the gym, not the playground
questions.explain: Loaded words like 'tired old' steer people toward yes; a fair version simply asks whether the playground should be replaced. The trap is calling a question fair just because answering no is still allowed.

questions.question: A school has 500 students. The council wants to know if students want a school hockey team, so it asks only the 25 students at hockey practice. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing is wrong; the sample would be fair if 500 were asked
The 25 asked all love hockey, so they cannot represent 500
Nothing is wrong; the question wording is neutral and polite
The council should have counted each student twice to be sure
questions.explain: Who you ask decides what you learn: 25 hockey players cannot speak for 500 students, so pick a random sample of the whole school. The trap is thinking that asking more people from the same keen group fixes it.

questions.question: A rec centre wants to know how busy its pool is. Staff counted the swimmers only on Monday mornings, for four weeks in a row. What is the main problem?
options: Nothing is wrong; four weeks of data is a large enough sample
Nothing is wrong; counting people can never be biased at all
Monday mornings are quiet, so busy times were never counted
The centre should also count how many staff work each day
questions.explain: Data collected at one time slot only describes that time slot, so count on different days and hours before saying how busy the pool is. The trap is thinking that repeating the same time slot for weeks cancels the timing bias.

questions.question: A class hands out 45 survey forms about school lunches. Before the lunch questions, each form asks the student to write their full name and their family's yearly income. What is the main problem?
options: The class should ask about breakfast instead of lunch
Nothing is wrong; the money question is worded politely
Nothing is wrong; 45 forms is enough to make results fair
Asking for name and income is private, so many skip it
questions.explain: Private questions about names and family income make students skip the form or answer untruthfully, which bends the results; keep sensitive questions optional and anonymous. Polite wording does not make a private question safe to ask.

questions.question: A student is writing a survey for Grade 9s about screen time. Which question is the least biased?
options: How many hours a day do you use a screen after school?
Don't you agree that too much screen time is harming teens?
Since 900 teens were asked, how bad is your screen habit?
How many hours do you waste staring at a screen each day?
questions.explain: A fair question uses neutral words and hints at no answer; 'Don't you agree', 'how bad' and 'waste' all push the person one way. The trap is thinking big numbers mentioned in the question make it fair.

questions.question: A school of 800 students wants to know whether the school day should start 30 minutes later. Which plan gives the least biased results?
options: Ask 400 students who arrive late, because more people is fairer
Ask 80 students drawn at random from the full student list
Ask 80 students 'Don't you want to sleep in 30 more minutes?'
Ask 80 students in the morning club that meets at 7:30 a.m.
questions.explain: Drawing names at random from the full student list gives every student an equal chance, so the sample mirrors the school. The trap is picking a group already tied to the topic, such as students who arrive late or a 7:30 club.

questions.question: A city surveyed bus riders only during July and August, then reported that bus use is low all year. Which change best fixes the flaw?
options: Survey 5000 riders in August so the sample is large
Ask in August, 'Don't you agree buses are rarely useful?'
Survey riders in several months across the whole year
Survey only drivers in August, since they see the buses
questions.explain: Summer data only describes summer, so spread the survey across months before making a claim about the whole year. The trap is thinking that adding thousands more summer riders repairs a timing problem.

questions.question: A school food survey lists only beef, pork and chicken as the foods you may pick, and it requires every student to write their religion. Which fix makes the survey fairest?
options: Keep the three foods and survey 600 students, not 60
Keep religion required and add 'Don't you love beef?'
Ask only students who eat meat, to save survey time
Add more food choices and make religion optional
questions.explain: A fair survey offers choices that fit everyone's diet and keeps personal items such as religion optional, so no student is pushed out. The trap is thinking a bigger sample fixes a form that some students cannot honestly answer.

questions.question: A radio station posts online: 'Do you agree that the new bike lane is a waste of money?' In two days 4200 people click, and 70% answer yes. The station reports that 70% of the city dislikes the bike lane. Which judgement is best?
options: Unsound: only volunteers replied and 'waste' steers answers
The report is sound because 4200 is a very large sample size
The report is sound because the question let people answer no
It is unsound only because a radio station is not a math group
questions.explain: Two faults stack: only people who chose to click replied, and the word 'waste' pushes them to yes, so the 70% cannot describe the city. A huge count never repairs a loaded question or a volunteer sample.

questions.question: A community centre serves about 3000 people across the week and must decide whether to add Sunday hours. Which plan gives the least biased answer?
options: Hand forms to everyone in the building on Saturday at 2 p.m.
Mail the form to 300 members picked at random from the list
Ask 300 members 'Don't you agree Sunday hours would help?'
Post the form online and use the first 1000 replies received
questions.explain: Mailing to members chosen at random from the full membership list reaches people whatever day or hour they normally visit. The trap is a plan that only catches one time slot, or one that lets people volunteer themselves.

questions.question: Maya surveys 1000 people leaving a hockey game about funding a new arena. Omar surveys 60 people picked at random from the city phone list. Whose results better represent the whole city?
options: Maya's, because 1000 people is far more than 60 people
Maya's, because hockey fans care most about the arena
Omar's, because his 60 were picked from the whole city
Neither, since a fair survey must ask 'Do you agree?' first
questions.explain: A small random sample of the whole city represents it better than a large sample of people already at a hockey game, because random picking gives everyone a chance. The trap is judging a survey by its size instead of by who was asked.

questions.question: A club reports: 'We asked 800 students, so our result has no bias.' In fact the form went only to students in the computer lab, and it asked 'Should our great coding club get more funding?' Which reason best explains the flaw?
options: There is no flaw because the word 'should' makes it a fair ask
The number 800 is wrong because no school can hold 800 forms
There is no flaw because 800 students cancels out any bias
Only lab users were asked and 'great' pushes people to agree
questions.explain: Bias enters twice here: the sample came from one room, and the praise word 'great' nudges agreement, so 800 replies still cannot be trusted. Sample size never cancels a loaded question or a narrow group.
